scope: four independent first-turn probes; not complete journeys

cases.name: newcomer_self
cases.message: I'm turning 65 next year and this is all new to me. I don't understand what Medicare is. Where do I start?
cases.expectation: Small useful foundation, no assumption of coverage or eligibility, at most one consequential next question.

proposed.reply:
Start with what Medicare is—not with choosing a plan. Medicare is health insurance from the federal government that helps pay for health care. It’s mainly for people 65 or older who meet its eligibility rules; some younger people qualify too.

The first two pieces to know are:
• Part A: hospital insurance, including inpatient hospital care.
• Part B: medical insurance, including doctor visits, outpatient care, tests and many preventive services.

Parts A and B together, run by the federal government, are called Original Medicare. You don’t need to learn every term at once; these two pieces give you a starting point.
proposed.question: Would it help to look next at the difference between Original Medicare and Medicare Advantage?

agenda_update.current_concern: Understand what Medicare is and where to start.

cases.name: caregiver_mixed
cases.message: I'm reviewing Mom's Original Medicare and supplement. I understand the premium is the monthly payment, but I don't understand what a deductible does. Keeping her doctors matters. How should we think about this?
cases.expectation: Distinguish understood premium from uncertain deductible; explain the latter and connect it to the coverage review, retaining doctor uncertainty.

proposed.reply:
For your mom’s review, separate two questions: what she could pay and whether she can keep her doctors.

A deductible is an amount you pay for care before coverage pays its share under that benefit’s rules. Unlike a premium, it isn’t a monthly payment just to have coverage. Copays and coinsurance are other costs when you use care.

To evaluate her Original Medicare and supplement together, we’d need the exact coverage terms—not just a published deductible—to understand her possible payments. Monthly premiums alone won’t show the total cost.

Doctor access needs its own check. Naming her doctors is a starting point, not confirmation that they participate under the coverage being considered. I haven’t verified her doctor access or personal costs.
proposed.question: Which doctors or hospitals would your mom want to keep?

agenda_update.current_concern: Understand deductibles and evaluate costs while preserving doctor access.

cases.name: experienced_self
cases.message: I'm reviewing my Medicare Advantage plan. I know the premium is what I pay monthly and copays are what I pay for care. Please skip the basics. I want help finding out if my cardiologist is in network next year.
cases.expectation: Honor the requested depth; work toward exact plan, year and clinician checks without asserting network participation.

proposed.reply:
We can skip the basics and focus on your cardiologist. I can help prepare a precise network check, but I can’t verify next year’s participation here because verified plan and provider sources aren’t available.

The check needs to match the exact plan, the cardiologist’s office location and next year—not just whether the office accepts the insurance company. Confirmation should come from both the plan and the office for that specific coverage period. A doctor’s name alone won’t establish network status.
proposed.question: What is your cardiologist’s name and the office location where you see them?

agenda_update.current_concern: Confirm whether the cardiologist is in network next year.

cases.name: confident_misconception
cases.message: I'm researching options for myself. I know a zero premium means all my medical care is free, so I just need a zero premium plan. Is that the right way to choose?
cases.expectation: Correct the cost misconception without shaming, explain a bounded distinction and avoid treating confidence as understanding or suggesting an unsupported plan.

proposed.reply:
Not quite—a zero plan premium does not mean free medical care. Wanting a lower monthly payment makes sense, but the premium is only one part of the cost.

• **Premium:** what you pay each month for coverage.
• **Deductible:** what you pay before coverage pays its share under the benefit’s rules.
• **Copays and coinsurance:** costs you pay when you use care.

A zero-premium plan can still have those costs when you see a doctor or receive treatment. So premium alone isn’t a sound way to choose: compare monthly payments alongside what you would pay for care, and check the exact plan’s doctors and prescription coverage. A published premium is not your personal total cost.
proposed.question: If a plan has no monthly premium but charges a copay for a doctor visit, would that visit necessarily be free?

agenda_update.current_concern: Whether a zero-premium plan means free medical care and is enough to choose coverage.
